summary.text: The innate immune system, also called the non-specific immune system, is the dominant immune response in plants, fungi, prokaryotes, and invertebrates.
In vertebrates it is one of two main immunity strategies, the other being the adaptive immune system.
It acts as a physical and chemical barrier to infectious agents and starts inflammatory responses that bring in immune cells at infection sites.

items.prompt: Your skin and the lining of your airways stop most germs from getting in. What role do they play?

options.label: A first line of defense most germs cannot cross
A second layer that learns each new germ
A store of antibodies kept for later use
A factory that makes new white blood cells

items.explain: Epithelial surfaces form a physical barrier that is impermeable to most infectious agents, acting as the first line of defense.

items.prompt: Your eyes water and your mouth stays moist. How do tears and saliva help protect you?

options.label: By teaching T cells to recognize germs
By hardening the skin
By flushing away infectious agents
By clotting the blood

items.explain: The flushing action of tears and saliva helps prevent infection of the eyes and mouth.

items.prompt: How can the normal bacteria living in your gut keep a harmful bacterium from settling in?

options.label: By building antibodies against it
By competing with it for nutrients and attachment sites
By vaccinating the gut wall
By shedding the skin that covers it

items.explain: Gut flora can prevent colonization by pathogens by secreting toxic substances or by competing for nutrients or cell surface attachment sites.

items.prompt: A biologist studies how a fungus defends itself against infection. Which immune strategy is the dominant one in it?

options.label: The adaptive strategy
The antibody strategy
The vaccine strategy
The innate strategy

items.explain: The innate immune system is the dominant response found in plants, fungi, prokaryotes, and invertebrates.

items.prompt: Inflammation puts up a physical barrier against infection spreading. What else does it do?

options.label: It promotes healing of damaged tissue
It builds an immunological memory
It makes new antibodies
It sheds the outer skin

items.explain: Inflammation establishes a physical barrier against the spread of infection and promotes healing of damaged tissue after the pathogen is cleared.

items.prompt: Where does the alarm that starts acute inflammation come from?

options.label: Antibodies delivered in by the bone marrow
Cells already in tissues, such as macrophages and mast cells
T cells that were produced after a first exposure
Vaccines that were given before the infection

items.explain: Acute inflammation is initiated by cells already present in all tissues, mainly resident macrophages, dendritic cells, histiocytes, Kupffer cells, and mast cells.
